title: The women of Saidpur
hook: a wedding photo in a ruined house: Guru Nanak's lament on ang 417 remembers the women as brides before it mourns what was done to them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Babarvani, and a tiger falling on a flock while the Master is asked to answer. Your line was he named the pain. Which ordinary person in the news did you stop for? Day one thousand one hundred sixty.

After a war, reporters walk through broken houses, and sometimes the camera stops on one thing left on a wall: a wedding photo. A bride in red, a groom beside her, everybody smiling. It says more than a casualty count. These were people with a before. In Raga Asa, on ang four seventeen, Guru Nanak sings a lament for the women caught in the invasion. Tradition ties it to Saidpur, the town of Bhai Lalo. And before the hymn mourns, it does something unexpected. It remembers their weddings.
screen: `A WEDDING PHOTO ON A BROKEN WALL.` → `PEOPLE WITH A BEFORE.` → `A LAMENT ON ANG 417.`

segments.voice: First, the before. In paraphrase, the hymn says: those heads that were lovely with braids, the parting of the hair filled with vermilion. And when they were married, their husbands looked handsome beside them. They came in palanquins decorated with ivory. Water was waved over their heads, and fans glittered beside them. Guru Nanak takes time over this. He lets us see them as brides, honored and celebrated, with husbands and households. Second, the after. The same heads, the hymn says, are now shorn, and dust is in their throats. They lived in palaces, and now they're not allowed even to sit near. Strings of pearls are broken, and ropes are put around their necks. He doesn't go further into what was done. He doesn't need to. The before makes the after unbearable. Third, why tell it this way. A lament that only counted the dead would make them a number. This one makes them people. Their wedding day is part of the record, kept right beside their suffering. That's a way of mourning that refuses to let war shrink anyone. Fourth, who is speaking. Guru Nanak is a man, singing about women, whose suffering could easily have been folded into someone else's story. He doesn't fold it in. He gives these women stanzas of their own, set in scripture, where they are still sung and read. That's who the women of Saidpur are on this path: not a footnote to the invasion, but people the Guru mourned with their before remembered. Today's line: he mourned them.
screen: `THE BEFORE: BRIDES IN PALANQUINS.` · `THE AFTER: DUST AND BROKEN PEARLS.` · `MOURNING THAT KEEPS THEM PEOPLE.` · `STANZAS OF THEIR OWN.` · then, large: `HE MOURNED THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor women who suffer in war. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind women living through war or its aftermath, in any place, in any time. Try not to see them only in the worst moment. Give each one a before: a kitchen, a classroom, a wedding, a job she was good at. Let that before stay beside whatever came after. If you pray, you can hold them before God in the way your tradition prays, or say Waheguru on each out-breath. If you don't, simply keep them company in your thoughts. The bell holds the time.
The women of Saidpur. Guru Nanak's lament on ang four seventeen, which remembers the women as brides, and mourns what the invasion did to them. Today's word.
Your line: he mourned them. Today, learn one real woman's name and story from a war, past or present, and tell it to someone with her before included. Day one thousand one hundred sixty.

howItsDone: This ashtpadi of Guru Nanak in Raga Asa is sung in kirtan as part of Gurbani, and some Sikhs recall it when remembering those who suffered in war and partition.
